judgments.title: Shaharun Bin Ab Lattif v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: HABEAS CORPUS Application for writ of habeas corpus - Preventive detention - Validity of detention order - Dangerous Drugs (Special Preventive Measures) Act 1985 ('Act 316') - Whether detention unlawful - Whether writ ought to be issued. DANGEROUS DRUGS Preventive detention - Detention order under s 6(1) Act 316 - Involvement in distribution of dangerous drugs - "Large group of people" - Public order - Minister's satisfaction - Whether requirements of Art 149 Federal Constitution satisfied. JUDICIAL REVIEW Scope of review - Preventive detention - Section 11C(1) Act 316 - Whether court limited to procedural non-compliance - Subjective satisfaction of Minister - Whether merits of investigation reviewable. DANGEROUS DRUGS Statement recording - Section 4(5) Act 316 - Read-back requirement - Whether statement read back to detainee - Whether detainee given opportunity to make corrections - Mandatory procedural requirement - Whether complied with. EVIDENCE Forgery - Alleged forged signatures on recorded statement - Burden of proof - Absence of expert evidence - Absence of police report - Presumption of regularity - Whether forgery proven. ADMINISTRATIVE LAW Mala fide - Conflict of interest - Alleged intimidation by investigating officers - Whether allegations substantiated - Affidavit evidence - Public officers performing official duties. DANGEROUS DRUGS Advisory Board - Representation hearing - Regulation 10(2)(b) Dangerous Drugs (Special Preventive Measures) (Advisory Board Procedure) Rules 1987 - Whether detainee denied right to be heard - Whether regulation ultra vires Act 316. DANGEROUS DRUGS Statutory reports - Delay in submission - Investigation report under s 3(3) - Inquiry Officer's report under s 5(4) - Whether delay constituted procedural non-compliance - Whether detention order invalidated. Held: Applicant failed to establish any material procedural non-compliance under Act 316; detention order valid; application for writ of habeas corpus dismissed.

delicti – Whether identity of exhibits produced in court was same as those seized from accused – Whether identity of exhibits was foundational and antecedent to proof of possession, knowledge and trafficking – Whether presumption of trafficking under s 37(da)(vi) engaged where identity of exhibits not established – Whether weight exceeding statutory threshold made weight discrepancy immaterial – Whether prosecution had made out prima facie case – Whether accused ought to be called to enter defence CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Close of prosecution's case – Section 180 of the Criminal Procedure Code – Prima facie case – Whether prosecution had adduced credible evidence proving each ingredient of offence – Maximum evaluation of prosecution evidence – Whether benefit of doubt at end of prosecution's case must go to accused – Whether discrepancies should be assessed cumulatively rather than in isolation – Whether court bound to consider possession and knowledge where foundational ingredient of identity not proved – Acquittal and discharge without defence being called EVIDENCE: Chain of custody – Drug exhibits – Whether chain of custody was unbroken – Whether identification of markings, dates and signatures alone sufficient to establish integrity of chain – Exhibits unmarked and unsealed between seizure and handover to investigating officer – Whether prosecution's witness's inconsistent account of when exhibits were weighed and marked affected integrity of chain – Whether inner packets directly enclosing drug material bearing no police marking weakened identity of exhibit – Unexplained thirty-minute discrepancy in time of handover of exhibits – Whether prosecution must explain gap in custody – Whether police weighing for classificatory purposes only EVIDENCE: Weight discrepancy – Unexplained increase in gross weight of drug exhibits between seizure and receipt by chemist – Whether unexplained increase in weight cast reasonable doubt on identity of exhibits – Whether difference in weighing apparatus adequate explanation where instruments were calibrated – Whether prosecution must explain discrepancy by expert evidence – Whether weight discrepancy explained by natural environmental factors where weight increased rather than decreased – Whether prosecution's duty to explain discrepancies – Whether search list recording no weight of exhibits was breach of safeguard designed for accused's protection – Whether markings recorded in search list before being physically applied to exhibits affected reliability of search list

judgments.title: Mohamad Nor Hafizudin Bin Mat Yusoff v Pendakwa Raya & ors

parties.label: PERAYU
names: Mohamad Nor Hafizudin Bin Mat Yusoff

judgments.catchwords: Criminal Appeal – Appeal against conviction and sentence from the Sessions Court under section 376(3) and section 377C of the Penal Code. Maximum Evaluation – Duty of the trial judge to conduct a positive evaluation of the prosecution's case at the close of the prosecution stage before calling for the defense. Prima Facie Case – Proof of credible evidence establishing each ingredient of the offense under section 173(h)(iii) of the Criminal Procedure Code. Credibility of Child Witness – Assessment of a 16-year-old victim's (SP8) testimony, emotional demeanor, and consistency despite lengthy cross-examination. Corroboration – Independent supporting evidence comprising medical findings (old tears on the hymen), psychiatric trauma records, eyewitness testimony of the victim's brother (SP6), and initial spontaneous disclosure via drawings to the school counselor (SP5). Discrepancies in Testimony – Legal principles concerning minor versus material discrepancies and the court's competency to accept parts of a witness's testimony. Bad Character Evidence – Prohibition against using bad character to link an accused to a charge, and the application of section 167 of the Evidence Act 1950 regarding independent sufficient evidence. Investigation Completeness – Effect of gaps or omissions in police investigation (SP9) on the core elements of the prosecuted charge. Alibi Defense – Substantive evaluation of alibi evidence, the credibility of interested witnesses (SD1, SD2, SD3), and the demeanor-based assessment of an independent witness (SD4). Notice of Alibi – Legal weight, procedural compliance, and the effect of delayed filing under section 402A of the Criminal Procedure Code. Standard of Proof & Reasonable Doubt – Application of the five-step framework in Mat v Public Prosecutor and the definition of a reasonable doubt. Sentencing Principles – Mandatory minimum sentences under section 376(3) and section 377C of the Penal Code, balancing mitigating factors against the breach of trust in incestuous child sexual abuse cases and public interest under the Sexual Offences Against Children Act 2017.
judgments.judge: YA Tuan Haji Azhar Bin Mokhtar

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case

judgments.title: BELLWORTH DEVELOPMENTS SDN BHD v SETIAKON BUILDERS SDN BHD
judgments.catchwords: The Court of Appeal reaffirmed the principle of minimal judicial intervention in arbitration. A procedural breach, such as an alleged one-day delay in submitting a draft award for AIAC technical review, does not automatically invalidate an arbitral award where the requirement is merely directory, no timely objection was raised, and no prejudice is shown. An arbitral award will not be set aside on the basis of a purported “new difference” where the issue was within the parties’ pleadings, evidence and submissions. Courts will not review the merits of an award under the guise of a setting-aside application.’
